Pressure. Force exerted per unit area, arising from molecules colliding with surfaces or from the gravitational weight of a fluid above. Measured in pascals, atmospheres, or bars, pressure is fundamental to understanding fluids, thermodynamics, and weather. Atmospheric pressure at sea level is approximately 101,325 pascals, decreases with altitude, and drives winds, weather patterns, and phase transitions. Pressure gradients are the engine of meteorology.

Pressure is defined as force divided by area. The standard international unit is pascal. One atmosphere equals approximately 760 millimeters of mercury. Pressure arises from molecular impacts on surfaces. According to kinetic theory, pressure is proportional to the number density of molecules times their average kinetic energy. The Ideal Gas Law relates pressure, volume, temperature, and mole count—pressures and volumes are related through this equation, though deviations occur near phase transitions and high pressures. Atmospheric pressure is the weight of the air column above a point and decreases exponentially with altitude, dropping to roughly ten percent of sea level pressure at sixteen kilometers. Pressure gradients are the fundamental driver of wind. Air flows from high-pressure anticyclones toward low-pressure cyclones, causing weather systems. Vapor pressure is the pressure exerted by a liquid-vapor equilibrium and increases with temperature. It determines the boiling point at any given pressure. Gauge pressure, the practical measure for tire and tank pressure, equals absolute pressure minus atmospheric pressure. Osmotic pressure governs water movement in cells, while hydrostatic pressure opposes osmotic flow in equilibrium. Blood pressure, typically 120 over 80 millimeters of mercury, must exceed osmotic pressure to prevent fluid accumulation in tissues. Deep-sea organisms withstand extreme pressure exceeding 1000 atmospheres because their proteins and lipids have evolved special adaptations to remain functional under such crushing force.
